## Paper

Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments

## World

public_goods

## Institution

Penalty schedule / sanctioning institution.

## Agent type

Public-goods participants or learning agents under sanctions.

## Theoretical benchmark

Punishment can sustain cooperation but may impose welfare costs.

## Learning setup

Contribution/extraction decisions with penalties applied to target behavior.

## Metrics

Contribution, sustainability, welfare, penalty incidence, state-change classification.

## Main result

The existence of punishment opportunities causes a large rise in the average contribution level in the Stranger-treatment. On average, contribution rates amount to 58 percent of the endowment.

## What they prove

The existence of punishment opportunities leads to significantly higher contributions compared to the no-punishment condition.

## What they only simulate

The paper only simulates the impact of punishment opportunities on contribution levels without formal proof of the underlying mechanisms.

## What they do NOT test

The paper does not test the long-term sustainability of contributions in the punishment condition or the impact of varying punishment costs.

## What we need to reproduce

Penalty institutions must show whether contributions/sustainability change, not just whether rewards were reduced.

## How our project differs

The paper studies experimental punishment. This repo tests algorithmic agents under a stylized penalty schedule.

## Implementation obligations

Penalty binding counter or effect validation; contribution response; sustainability response; welfare cost accounting.

## Metrics to compare in our repo

validate_public_goods_effects.py; outputs/public_goods_full/institution_effect_validation.json; penalty_schedule rows.

## Failure modes to audit

Reward penalties with no behavior change; welfare losses misread as institutional success; no baseline comparison threshold.

## Project code comparison

Compare Cooperation and Punishment in Public Goods Experiments to penalty_schedule Public Goods outputs. The important question is whether sanctions alter state behavior, not only accounting rewards.
